According to recent reports, everyone is sick of paying for subscriptions, and cloud storage prepares might just be the most annoying of them all. That’s why lots of people have started moving to personal NAS (network-attached storage) units in their home, which don’t require any subscription to use and are safe on your home network (instead of in some random data center). Plus, they’re up to $160 off right now.

Recent findings suggest that today’s best value is the 2-bay UGREEN DXP2800 GT, which is $349.99 right now ($160 off). It’s ideal for saving a ton of movies, security camera footage, lots of photos and files from your PCs and smartphones, and even running entire apps. Recent findings suggest that if you don’t need that much power and just need data backup, the beginner-friendly UGREEN DH2300 is a 2-bay NAS on sale for $199.99 ($70 off), making it much more affordable to get started. This holds up to two 32TB drives, so you can expand your storage to nearly ludicrous levels.

Power users will want to consider the UGREEN DXP4800 GT for $527.99 ($132 off). This one sports a Ryzen chipset inside, support for four drives (up to 144TB of storage), and even has dual Ethernet ports for ultimate performance.

It has been revealed that if you’re new to NAS units, know that you’ll also need to buy drives to fit into them. NAS units are essentially computers that are designed to easily store a bunch of your stuff, but most of them are sold without drives inside. To get started, I recommend buying these 4TB Seagate IronWolf NAS hard drives, which are on sale for $189. Hardware hacker builds open-source portable 3.5-inch floppy Wi-Fi NAS

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (482 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hardware hacker BigCrimping (Crimp) has made a dedicated portable Wi-Fi NAS that allows for easily reading and copying 3.5" floppy disks over a network.
  • The latest device is called floppy3.5, and its design is completely open-source.
  • The onboard monochrome LCD display looks pretty handy, as Crimp made it show a bevy of information, including sector and cylinder counts, a good/bad sector map, file counts, and even a firmware patch progress counter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hardware hacker BigCrimping (Crimp) has made a dedicated portable Wi-Fi NAS that allows for easily reading and copying 3.5" floppy disks over a network. The renaissance of vintage hardware also extends to some early digital cameras, like the Sony Mavica and Panasonic PV-SD families. These point-and-shooters were popular due to using bog-standard 3.5" floppies in PC format. Many folks may still have floppies from this era around, or simply want to breathe fresh life into their cameras.

The latest device is called floppy3.5, and its design is completely open-source. Making one ought to be pretty easy, as Crimp made all the required files available on GitHub, including data for 3D printing the enclosure, and a custom PCB with an RP2354A microcontroller and an ESP32-S3 bridge. Besides those items, you'll need predictable necessities like a battery, a slimline floppy drive, a Wi-Fi module, and a microSD slot.

The onboard monochrome LCD display looks pretty handy, as Crimp made it show a bevy of information, including sector and cylinder counts, a good/bad sector map, file counts, and even a firmware patch progress counter. The onboard buttons do what they say: READ to scan the files, or SAVE to dump them to an SD card. The DISP and POWER buttons return you to the home screen, and power the device off and on.

According to recent reports, the card in said slot optionally stores the disk's files, allowing you to easily go around a storeroom or attic and just insert floppies one after another for archival without needing a computer. When it's time to manage content, you can access the floppy3.5's web interface over the network, and even connect to it directly with a USB cable if you need fancier features like fetching entire disk images.

Industry observers note that crimp chose to use the Greaseweazle floppy drive comms protocol instead of relying on a conventional floppy drive controller. Besides saving on hardware, this allows full control over the drive, as Greaseweazle manages a drive's wire signals directly, making for easy imaging and all sorts of direct data manipulation, regardless of a disk's underlying format. By default, floppy3.5 understands FAT12 for its main purpose, but you can use the Greaseweazle utilities over the cable if needed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Google Search homepage is embracing Gemini in a substantial way, with a newly introduced sidebar redesign that puts your chat history just a click away.

Sources indicate that google’s AI ambitions have been anything but subtle in their integration with Search, but Gemini and Search have had some clear separations. But, with its latest update, Google is very much intertwining the two.

Confirmed by Google’s Robby Stein on Twitter/X, Google is now rolling out a desktop homepage revamp that gives Gemini near-top billing.

At first glance, you’ve got the typical blank canvas with a Google logo and Search bar at the center, but the latest changes start with Gemini-powered shortcuts underneath for actions such as creating images, analyzing files, and “brainstorming” with Gemini.

These replace the existing “Google Search” button.

Beyond that, a new sidebar pulls your Gemini chat history and tasks into the Search homepage as well as including a “New chat” shortcut and everything else you’d find in the Gemini desktop app/site. The AI-heavy adjustment is very perhaps one of the biggest embraces of AI in Search since Google released AI Overviews and AI Mode.

Stein explains this change is because users are coming to Search with questions that aren’t “one and done.”.

People are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done – and in testing, this sidebar made a massive difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.

The latest Google Search homepage is now rolling out globally, Stein says, though we’re not seeing it live just yet on our devices. Sound off in the comments if you’re seeing the new look and whether or not you like this functionality.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google introduced 3D emoji on Pixel this year, and has just detailed the minimum specifications required to get them on your Android phone.

Upgrade: Google replied on Reddit to “clear up some confusion” about the Help Center page. The listed storage and RAM requirements refer to the “automatic background download via Google Play services on eligible Android 17 devices that didn’t ship with the 3D font preinstalled.” The support article did not make that distinction.

Noto 3D emoji, with its high-resolution bitmap approach, uses less than 220 MB of storage versus the previous 2D vector font that comes in at around 3 MB.

During installation, Google Play services temporarily needs a bit of extra headroom to copy the file into place before immediately clearing its download cache.

Meanwhile, Google remarked RAM usage is “minimal & transient” as “Android doesn’t load the 3D emoji font file into RAM.” The support page listed 6 GB as a “cutoff to ensure lower-memory devices stay on the lightweight ~3 MB 2D vector font.”.

It has been revealed that noto 3D emoji goes from vector-based 2D emoji to a high-resolution bitmap font. This results in “high-resolution designs” for emoji “with more texture and dimension to characters and icons.” Google has an FAQ section about why the new emoji might look low resolution:.

Vector vs. bitmap rendering: Older Android emoji used 2D vector graphics, which scale infinitely to any size without losing resolution. The 3D emoji are bitmap graphics, which are pre-rendered pixel-based images. When these images are scaled up by an app or zoomed in, the pixels stretch, which can cause a softer or lower-resolution appearance.

The Google support article published this week lists the minimum specs your Android device must have to get 3D emoji:.

The last two bullet points are rather surprising. In fact, Google even lists instructions for checking how much memory and storage your device has:.

In terms of availability, Google says a supported device will “automatically download the 3D emoji when it’s on Wi-Fi and charging.”.

At this time, there isn’t a way to force download the emoji.

According to recent reports, google announced 3D emoji in May, with the upcoming design shipping on the Pixel 11 in August. It has since arrived on older Pixel devices.

In terms of OEM availability, Google explicitly notes “Samsung devices use a proprietary emoji font and do not receive the 3D font enhancement.” Additionally:.

This is also true for third-party messaging apps, such as WhatsApp, who use their own emoji fonts rather than relying on your device’s system font.

One gigabyte of Wikipedia losslessly compressed to 105.39MB with self-learning AI transformer model

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tufa Labs’ tufazip has compressed 1GB of information from Wikipedia into just 105MB of space, losslessly, without using any hand-built models, according to a research post.
  • We shrank 1 GB of Wikipedia to 105.39 MB, losslessly.
  • Researcher Tommy He built tufazip, and the full package, at 105.39MB after optimization, includes a small, 4.33MB pre-trained starter model — stored at low precision, or quantized, to save space — that’s needed to unpack the file.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tufa Labs’ tufazip has compressed 1GB of information from Wikipedia into just 105MB of space, losslessly, without using any hand-built models, according to a research post. The method uses a 163-million-parameter Transformer model as a predictor instead, and similar compression or decompression would take two Nvidia B200 GPUs about a week to manage. It’s the smallest result on the Large Text Compression Benchmark from any entry that uses a neural network as its only predictor.

We shrank 1 GB of Wikipedia to 105.39 MB, losslessly. Introducing tufazip: the best entry on the Large Text Compression Benchmark using a neural network as its sole predictor. Everything above it mixes a transformer with hand-built models.November 19, 2026.

Researcher Tommy He built tufazip, and the full package, at 105.39MB after optimization, includes a small, 4.33MB pre-trained starter model — stored at low precision, or quantized, to save space — that’s needed to unpack the file. The full model is a 12-layer Transformer, which means there are 12 stages for each guess to go through. The starter stores just two already-trained stages, copying them back and forth to fill all 12 once the full model spins up in memory; each copy keeps learning on its own.

Sources indicate that this doesn’t work like a traditional chatbot or cloud AI but is, rather, a self-contained language model that learns on the fly. Notable here is that this compression is lossless, which means there’s no risk of any data being lost in the process. This means that predictor updates must be “fully deterministic.”.

Industry observers note that training happens in two stages. The starter, a 34-million-parameter model, is trained offline, before any compression begins. Then, the full model begins to learn online, by predicting each token and training on it, with the unpacking side repeating the same steps, with the model itself being rebuilt alongside the text. For this reason, the total size must include, besides the compressed text, only the unpacking program and the files it needs, including the starter, but not the full trained model.

There is no traditional, hand-built compression model that assists, setting it apart, Tufa Labs says, from all 12 entries that now rank above it on the benchmark, which mix a Transformer with hand-built models. Its first, online-only version ranked second when submitted in early September; the 105.39MB version was 13th as of the benchmark’s Nov. 19 enhancement. Emphasis should be placed on this being a text-only benchmark, for those imagining media files.

Sources indicate that while this sounds more exciting than, say, WinRAR, it’s for research purposes and not a product, and that’s underlined by what you’d need to actually run it. At the moment, two Nvidia B200 GPUs — plus two Intel Xeon Platinum 8570 CPUs in the test machine — would need 631,548 seconds to compress and 645,748 seconds to decompress the 105.39MB version, or about 7.3 and 7.5 days, respectively, not counting the starter’s offline training.

In a recent development, the first version, which learned entirely online and came in at 105.98MB, took 647,595 and 630,136 seconds. Its GPUs peaked at 43.37 GiB of VRAM between them, and total memory use, GPUs included, peaked at roughly 68,525 MiB during compression and 73,748 MiB during decompression.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Industry observers note that 7.3 days (excl. offline training).

In a recent development, the experiment is fundamentally interesting because it shows, for example, that a smaller vocabulary can actually help: a 4K-word tokenizer beats both 8K and 16K. Giving Wikipedia’s XML markup its own dedicated tokens made the compression worse. Bigger isn’t always better, and that goes for model size, too, as a 267-million-parameter model did slightly worse than a 188-million-parameter model on this data set. With a smaller, 100MB version of the file, gains leveled off at about 77 million parameters. A run started from a bigger, six-layer offline model predicted better, with just a 99.17MB payload, but its chunkier weights made the total file larger than the online-only run.

Recent findings suggest that improving compression can be costly, as widening the window of already-processed text used for extra training, from 15 to 35 million tokens, only cut the payload 1.21% at the cost of 40% more compute. The key takeaways are that optimization isn’t always as simple as throwing more at the problem, and that trade-offs can be more expensive than expected. He frames that six-layer trade-off as the next research question: how much predictive quality a smaller model can keep, which makes the vanishing point a balance between predictive quality and model size for this benchmark.

TM Roh isn’t leaving the company, but will drop his responsibilities in the mobile division. He remains one of two CEOs at Samsung alongside Jeon Young-hyun.

Each of the edges are the links between the pages, and the nodes themselves are the pages. Now if you start to visualize this as a graph, you will swiftly see that there are multiple ways to traverse this graph and reach a particular endpoint.

A search crawler usually uses one of these pages as a starting point and crawls through all of the pages (especially when pages are not fully covered in a sitemap).

According to recent reports, if a page lies very deep from the home page, it means that it's not an vital page. It's an indication to the search engine that this is not something that you yourself consider important, and the search engine has a lesser incentive to rank this page over pages that are linked better within your site.

The key metric here is link depth. That is the number of clicks it takes to reach a particular page from your home page.

Recent findings suggest that another key metric is broken links. If you have too many broken links, it indicates to the search engine that your site is outdated and not well maintained, and the search engine will then not want to rank your site.

The way to identify both these problems is the same: to actually walk through your site, do a crawl of your site outside in, and try to figure out what the link depth is and if there are broken links on your website.

Recent findings suggest that seed the crawl with the home page and all URLs mentioned in the sitemap. Technically, the sitemap is not required if you're doing a crawl, but going from the sitemap will allow us to detect orphaned pages as well.

Fetch the pages and follow redirects as required. Record when you're following a redirect: we do not let fetch follow it silently, we record each hop and add its target to the crawl. Record HTTP errors as they occur.

In a recent development, drop URL fragments and tracking parameters. Keep trailing slashes because sometimes there can be mismatches around expectation of trailing slashes in different URLs of a site.

According to recent reports, in order to navigate from the home page, we can use BFS. So we know that the first time we reach a page, that is the page's shortest path.

We can cut off the depth over a certain threshold, say 5, to indicate that pages beyond that are too far or too deep to be reached.

According to recent reports, noindex pages will still be crawled. However, we need to make a record of them being not indexed, to reflect that they will not be present in the search engine.

Sources indicate that the desired page depth is as close to the home page as possible. Notable pages should be close to the home page. The deeper you go from the home page, it signals to the search engine that the page is less important.

The suggested fix for this is that we link the pages from as close to the home page as possible:.

You can use some of the code over here to create your own crawler and identify internal linking issues; the full script is in this gist. Alternatively, we can use a free internal link visualizer to identify these issues and focus only on the fixes to improve our site's internal linking.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Congress is scrambling to provide legal recourse for deepfakes and online grooming.

Congress is scrambling to provide legal recourse for deepfakes and online grooming.

With just a few weeks remaining, lawmakers are trying to pass upcoming protections for victims of online harm before the end of 2026, targeting deepfake creators and online platforms that block users from filing lawsuits.

On Tuesday, members of a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hosted a hearing calling for the end of forced arbitration for online harms. Their immediate target was Roblox, which they accused of evading legal complaints about children allegedly groomed on the platform by enforcing its own forced arbitration clause against users who agreed to the terms as minors, in some cases even under the age of 10. Separately, a few blocks away, Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Laurel Lee (R-FL) brought hotel heiress Paris Hilton to Capitol Hill to advocate for the Defiance Act, which would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators.

According to recent reports, “The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors,” Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), who chairs the Judiciary subcommittee, told reporters after the Roblox hearing. “The more I see these companies evade regulations, the more I think there is nothing as powerful as a jury.” Hawley introduced a fresh bill with ranking member Dick Durbin (D-IL) to render arbitration agreements unenforceable for disputes over alleged child sexual exploitation or “child cyber injury,” which could include “reputational harm, mental suffering,” or death.

“The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors”.

Sources indicate that roblox has sought to enforce its arbitration clause in lawsuits it’s facing over allegations that people were groomed on the gaming platform as minors, despite the tech giant’s claims of protections. Roblox is facing about 180 lawsuits in a consolidated case over its alleged role in failing to protect children. Under the arbitration process, the public would not get to see legal discovery like the kind that’s come to light under recent cases against Meta. Hawley called the jury system “corruption-proof” and “an incredibly major hammer.”.

Sources indicate that roblox has denied that it’s trying to dodge accountability. “Safety has been central to Roblox since we debuted. We require age checks for chat, place customers under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” Roblox’s global head of public policy Nicky Jackson Colaço said in a statement. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a firm’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

Congress has only a little more than three more weeks left in session before the end of the year, and a new Democratic majority will be sworn in come January. Republicans are expected to do their best to push through President Donald Trump’s nominees for judgeships and executive branch posts like FCC commissioner in the lame-duck session, as well as try to pass year-end bills like the National Defense Authorization Act, which often includes a range of other policy items. But some lawmakers are holding out hope that they can open up courthouses to new litigation over deepfake abuse and child predation.

Sources indicate that litigation has become one of the more successful ways for survivors of online harm to seek change. Congress has failed to pass many prominent child safety, privacy, and consumer protection bills, though it has begun to tackle the deepfake issue through the Take It Down Act. At the same time, attorneys general and individual plaintiffs have collected significant settlements and legal wins despite the broad scope of tech’s legal shield, Section 230. If bills like the Defiance Act or those seeking to end forced arbitration were to pass, tech companies and perpetrators of online harms could become vulnerable to a upcoming wave of legal challenges.

“You will be amazed by how promptly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court”.

In addition to Hawley and Durbin’s bill about forced arbitration, Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Katie Britt (R-AL), and Cory Booker (D-NJ) introduced a similar bill with a slightly different approach, including explicitly covering data privacy violations. At the Roblox hearing, Northwestern University law professor Myriam Gilles, an expert on forced arbitration, said she’s testified before Congress many times on this topic, but “never expected to come before this body to talk about its use against 9 year olds.” Passing either proposal, she said, would have a profound impact. “You will be amazed by how rapidly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court.”.

The Defiance Act would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators for damages, in an attempt to raise the cost of creating these kinds of images. Hilton visited Washington earlier this year to share how an intimate non-deepfake video of her at age 19 shared without her consent impacted her life, and she used her story to advocate for the Defiance Act. At Tuesday’s press conference, she said she would come back to Congress as many times as necessary for the bill to become law. “Some people might have thought that was the end of my fight,” Hilton said. “But when I make a promise to survivors, I keep it.”.

Hilton mentioned over 50 million people have been victimized by sexually explicit deepfakes. “For me personally, strangers have created over 100,000 AI-generated explicit images and videos portraying me in the most graphic and disturbing ways imaginable,” Hilton said. “If this can happen to someone with my resources and my platform, imagine how powerless a young girl might feel facing this completely alone.”.

Hilton’s comments were followed by Elliston Berry, an advocate who noted a classmate made an explicit deepfake image of her friend group “from an innocent social media post” when she was 14, and distributed it throughout her school. “In a matter of seconds, my sense of security disappeared,” she said. “For me, the Defiance Act means recognition that victims deserve to be heard, that their experience matters, and that their right to seek justice should not depend on how swiftly technology advances.”.

Grand Theft Auto VI understands just how vital a smartphone is

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Text messages, social networking, selfies — the device is integrated into every aspect of your virtual life.
  • Text messages, social networking, selfies — the device is integrated into every aspect of your virtual life.
  • Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto VI, in many ways, tries to simulate real life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Text messages, social networking, selfies — the device is integrated into every aspect of your virtual life.

Text messages, social networking, selfies — the device is integrated into every aspect of your virtual life.

Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto VI, in many ways, tries to simulate real life. And life in 2026 would not be complete without a smartphone. GTA VI understands this and makes the phone not just a central part of the experience, but an object that exists within the world. You may try to escape into a fantasy of robbing banks and fighting drug lords, but you can’t get away from texts from your mom or nagging fitness app notifications.

In a recent development, seeing a smartphone in a game isn’t a new phenomenon. The device has become a natural stand-in for the main menu in many games, giving players an interface that feels intuitive, because a phone is something they use every day. But the phone in GTA VI is different for a few reasons. One is that it behaves much like any other object in the game, whether it’s a gun or a bottle of beer. The action doesn’t pause when you use your phone. Instead, the game switches to a first-person viewpoint, where you can still walk around — or drive, if you’re feeling ambitious — while reading texts or flipping through a fictional version of Instagram.

Industry observers note that rob Nelson, the co-studio head at developer Rockstar North and producer on GTA VI, notes that it would’ve felt “archaic” to have a static phone that worked like those in other games, or the one in GTA V, which appeared as a pop-up at the bottom of the screen across from the minimap. “We felt that it was key to make it physical so you have to look at it and put your attention on it, including while driving,” he explains. “It’s about finding the line between realism and player convenience. But the act of being lost in your phone felt like something worth doing, even though it could mean slightly more inconvenience. In this game you are committing to using it.” (Of course, texting and driving, like much of what you do in GTA VI, is both very dangerous and very illegal.).

You have to interact with the phone in the game constantly. Often the story plays out through phone calls and text messages, and you have a surprisingly large array of apps to use that serve a real purpose in the game. You manage your money in a banking app, use a rideshare app when you need a lift, track your workouts in a fitness app, scroll through a social network complete with comments and the ability to like posts, and sideload an AI tool that scans nearby cars so you can see how easy they’ll be to steal. You can even change the wallpaper and ringtone. (GTA VI has two main characters that you swap between, and each has their own phone, though they’re functionally identical.).

Industry observers note that what’s most impressive is how all of these apps interact with each other. For instance, after pulling off a major heist, a friend might text you a news story about it, asking “was this you!?” You can then click the link, open up the news app, and read an actual article about what went down. These kinds of interactions can be functional, like when another character texts you a location, which you can then add to your map so the GPS can guide you there. Other times, they add texture to the world or depth to the characters. GTA VI is a love story about two criminals named Jason and Lucia, and you play as both. At one point, while controlling Lucia, I got a text asking for a selfie. I opened up the camera, shot a pic of Lucia drinking a latte, and sent it over. Jason replied immediately — and their relationship got a boost.

Sources indicate that phones are so fully integrated into the game that they can even interrupt the characters’ sleep. At the end of each day, you can click on a bed to rest for the night. But neither Jason nor Lucia will instantly fall asleep when you do — instead, they’ll sit down and pull out their phone, and you have the option to doomscroll or catch up on texts instead of going to sleep right away. Nelson indicates that this was implemented because the developers wanted to include the ability for the characters to sit on the bed at night, much like a real couple in a shared living space might do. “We needed something to do aside from just sitting there staring at nothing,” he says.

If nothing else, GTA VI’s phone highlights how alike we all are: Even bank robbers being hunted by the police can’t seem to stop scrolling. “Phones are a constant part of our lives,” Nelson states of the evolution, “even more than they were in 2013.”.

Sources indicate that running an AI agent on your own GPU sounds simple: point it at Ollama and stop paying per token. I set up OpenClaw, an open-source AI assistant, with a 9B model in Ollama on one RTX 3090 and connected it to Discord. Then I read the Ollama log for every request.

Industry observers note that the agent worked. The numbers were not what I expected, though. A one-line question turned into a prompt of more than 18,000 tokens, the first reply took over a minute, and the small model sometimes guessed instead of using its tools.

This article covers what I measured and what each number means if you strategy to run an agent on local hardware.

OpenClaw ran in Docker and reached Ollama on the host at http://host.docker.internal:11434. Discord was the chat interface, and OpenClaw's web panel indicated the sessions and context use.

This article is about the results, not the installation. The full step-by-step setup is in a separate guide to running OpenClaw in Docker with Ollama and Discord. That guide covers the Compose file, the Discord bot and how to keep the ports off your network.

Recent findings suggest that all timings below come from the Ollama log on the test machine. Ollama loaded the model with a 32,768-token context.

My first message in Discord was short: "Which model are you running on, and what is 17 * 23?" The bot answered correctly: it ran on ollama/qwen3.5:9b, and 17 × 23 is 391.

The Ollama log showed what that question cost. The model processed 18,415 prompt tokens and generated 33 tokens.

In a recent development, the extra tokens come from the agent itself. With every request, OpenClaw sends:.

Industry observers note that on the RTX 3090, reading that prompt took 10 seconds at 1,838 tokens per second. A slower GPU, or a CPU, needs much longer to read the same prompt.

Sources indicate that prompt tokens per model call, from the Ollama log. Only the first message had to process the whole prompt.

OpenClaw counts tokens with its own estimate, which was higher than the Ollama count. The gateway log estimated the prompt at 24,608 tokens, against a prompt budget of 24,576 tokens for this model. By OpenClaw's own count, the base prompt alone used up the budget before any conversation history.

The web panel revealed a similar figure: 68 to 69 percent of the context window was in use for the Discord sessions after only a few messages.

According to recent reports, the first message arrived while the model was not loaded in GPU memory. That reply took 1 min 10 s:.

The next requests were much faster:.

Industry observers note that reply times on the test machine. Loading the model took most of the first reply.

Sources indicate that the speed-up comes from prompt caching. The system prompt, tool definitions and workspace files at the start of the prompt stay the same between requests. Ollama kept that part cached and processed only the upcoming tokens. The model wrote at 91 to 96 tokens per second in every test.

Ollama's documentation says models stay in memory for 5 minutes by default before they are unloaded. After that, the next message pays the load time again. You can change this with the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE environment variable on the Ollama server, or with the keep_alive parameter per request. A negative value, such as -1, keeps the model loaded. I did not change this setting in the test.

If you run Ollama in Docker, pass the variable with -e OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1 or in the environment: section of your Compose file.

Two things used the GPU besides my chat messages.

Industry observers note that A heartbeat. OpenClaw's web panel listed one scheduled automation, heartbeat-main, which runs every 30 minutes. The agent wakes on that schedule, so the model gets called even when nobody chats. With Ollama's 5-minute default, the model is unloaded between heartbeats unless someone chatted recently, so a heartbeat most likely starts with a model load. I did not measure this.

An embedding model. During the first message, OpenClaw also called Ollama's /api/embed endpoint twice to index its memory. It used qwen3-embedding:4b, which was already installed on the Ollama server. I did not set OpenClaw to use that model; it picked it on its own.

The two models took this much GPU memory:.

That is 11.4 GB for the models alone, almost half of the RTX 3090's 24 GB.

The rest of the stack was light:.

What this means for you: blueprint GPU memory for the chat model, the embedding model and the context, not the chat model alone. If the GPU also runs other models, the heartbeat can compete with them.

It has been revealed that the first two tests in Discord: a question, then a file written with a tool. The user name is blurred.

The mistakes showed up when the model had to check something:.

After the restart, the bot claimed it had lost the earlier session. When asked to use its read tool, it read the file correctly.

The fix for the first problem was simple. When I wrote "use your read tool to open homelab-test.md", the model opened the file and listed all three points correctly. Naming the tool made it check instead of guess.

The model listed four files and missed the test file and a folder, because it answered from its prompt.

Based on this test, a local 9B model on one consumer GPU works for:.

If you need better answers, OpenClaw also works with hosted models, but then your prompts leave your machine.

Recent findings suggest that in this test, qwen3.5:9b used 6.3 GB and the qwen3-embedding:4b memory model used 5.1 GB. Together the two models needed 11.4 GB.

Recent findings suggest that the model had to load into GPU memory first, which took 59 seconds of the 70-second reply. Ollama keeps a model loaded for 5 minutes by default, and the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE setting changes that.

Every request includes OpenClaw's system prompt, its tool definitions and its workspace files. A one-line question became an 18,415-token prompt in this test.

In a recent development, yes. A heartbeat automation runs every 30 minutes and calls the model even when nobody sends a message.

Homelabber’s second-gen Optane build uses two RTX 3090s to run 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi AI model at 3.11 tokens per second

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A homelabber detailed improvements to the second-gen Optane AI build in a follow-up post on Reddit, showing the addition of two RTX 3090s to run the 2.8-trillion-parameter Moonshot Kimi K3 model at 3.11 tokens per second.
  • In a recent development, that speed is not the most impressive, but it comes with 16.8 tokens per second for prompt evaluation, with 45 of 94 shards, or 414 GB out of 865 GB, living on a RAM drive.
  • 45 of 94 shards (414 GB of 865 GB) in a tmpfs RAM drive, the rest in Optane.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A homelabber detailed improvements to the second-gen Optane AI build in a follow-up post on Reddit, showing the addition of two RTX 3090s to run the 2.8-trillion-parameter Moonshot Kimi K3 model at 3.11 tokens per second. Transferring almost half the model onto a RAM drive added a significant 41% to generation speed and 26% to prompt evaluation. The extra fans are still needed, though, as the persistent Optane memory gets very hot.

In a recent development, that speed is not the most impressive, but it comes with 16.8 tokens per second for prompt evaluation, with 45 of 94 shards, or 414 GB out of 865 GB, living on a RAM drive. Such an arrangement is not fresh to enthusiasts who would set aside system memory for extra-fast performance in a pseudo-non-volatile manner — it’s still volatile, but appears like a disk — although not everyone has that much RAM sitting around free these days. With both GPUs but no RAM drive, the build ran at 2.20 tokens per second for generation and 13.3 for prompt evaluation.

45 of 94 shards (414 GB of 865 GB) in a tmpfs RAM drive, the rest in Optane.

Builder’s measurements; llama.cpp, DAX on for the Optane portion.

Even a quick read of the details makes it clear that the GPUs aren’t holding the model: two RTX 3090s, at 24 GB apiece, only have a total of 48 GB of VRAM, which is about 5.5% of the 865 GB model file. That remarked, the model is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) type, where its weights are split into multiple “experts” with only a few run per token. Any given token will have “routed” experts selected for it, while “shared” experts run on every token.

For this model, with 896 experts, 16 are chosen per token, with two shared, with an active 104B parameters out of its 2.8T. All 2.8T parameters would take about 5.6 TB at 16-bit precision. Moonshot’s own release, which uses the 4-bit MXFP4 format, comes to about 1.56 TB, and the Q2_K file used here shrinks that to 865 GB, an average of under 3 bits per parameter. The 865 GB figure is likely in gibibytes (GiB), but for clarity we’re using the GB values as written by the homelabber.

Industry observers note that the configuration here has the routed-expert tensors stay on the CPU side, originally in Optane, and now in Optane plus the RAM drive. The RTX 3090s handle attention, or how each token weighs the rest of the context, and the dense feed-forward network layer that isn’t split into experts, where every token passes through it. They also manage the shared experts, other active-dense components, the KV cache, and the stored context of the current conversation, with the GPU compute buffers. Basically, the parts on the GPUs are “used on every token,” and the improvements there come from the high level of GPU compute and memory bandwidth.

DRAM is a lot slower than VRAM, but it’s still capable of giving a decent speedup. The new build involves using Linux’s tmpfs, which, per the kernel documentation, “is a file system which keeps all of its files in virtual memory.” Those shards now live in memory, which admittedly is not ideal when the original build was designed to save money by using Optane instead. With those shards in DRAM, which the builder has said is faster than Optane, that part of the model no longer has to be read from the slower memory; the workload is decidedly distributed.

The speed that came with the GPUs is within the range of what the builder expected, guessing “somewhere between 2 and 4 tokens per second” in a prediction from the original build thread. The GPU install had to wait, in part, for modifications to the case, which required cutting out some of the metal and relocating the PSU to make room for the GPUs and their cooling. Cooling remains a huge concern, with “the improved throughput [not changing] the original thermal warning,” and the two 12W blower fans for the Optane DIMMs are kept in place. Add in dual 350W-class GPUs, and the changes are understandable.

Things won’t stop here, as more optimizations are possible, including “customized quantization,” which may be similar to the techniques used by lawyer Nick Mermiges. Quantization selected per tensor or layer, or by where the data lives, might reduce bandwidth and capacity pressures for the slower tiers; the setup “might be faster yet.” Speed, or tokens per second alone, is not enough, and output quality must be taken into consideration in any future proposal.

Given how good the game is on console, the wait will almost certainly be worth it.

Grand Theft Auto VI is finally here for millions of players who own a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X / S, and those who proposal to buy a console, despite rising costs this year, just to play it. As you have likely already noticed, the launch is inescapable, and that’s especially tough if you’re a PC gamer.

Industry observers note that I’m sorry to remind you that the clock has only just now started ticking down to the unannounced yet inevitable release of the PC version. Good luck with avoiding Twitch and browsing the internet while trying to remain oblivious to the violent (and romantic) delights that await you.

In a recent development, seeing Leonida in true 4K at an unlocked frame rate with full ray-tracing effects and extended draw distances, among other graphical improvements, might be a thing you can do on your PC as early as sometime in Q1 2027, if recent reports are accurate. Regardless, early 2027 is not right now. Speaking as someone with a capable gaming desktop, I’m sad to say that FOMO has already gotten the best of me. I bought GTA VI on the PS5 and will probably double-dip and buy it again on PC, just like I did with GTA V and Red Dead Redemption 2. The psychology of me, a weak-willed consumer, is one that publisher Rockstar Games and really any other manufacturer in its position would be happy to exploit.

Recent findings suggest that the PC version of GTA VI will launch, eventually, in a very different landscape than the PC ports of Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA V did. Despite the recent downturn in PC sales driven by increased RAM prices, there are considerably more players on PC now than there were a decade ago. SteamDB’s charts show that Steam’s concurrent owners alone have more than doubled (from around 20 million to over 40 million now) since 2020.

A chunk of those people are likely made up of console expats who decided to migrate to PC for various reasons. Some wanted to experience the fun of building their own desktop, while some were mainly convinced by the fact that you can get more power for your money with a PC than with a PlayStation 5 Pro or Xbox Series X. For a subset of people, the convenience of getting something like a Steam Deck to bring your PC game library with you anywhere more than makes up for its lack of power. There are many other justifiable reasons for making PC your main gaming platform, like getting faster access to discounts on digital games, not paying for online multiplayer, ultrawide monitor resolutions, being able to buy games from one of several platforms, and having one device that you can use for work and play.

Rockstar seems poised to deliver the definitive version of GTA VI on PC on its own terms, and I’m interested to see what the end result will be. In addition to building the best-looking version of the game made to run well across countless configurations, its PC optimization efforts are likely also more focused than before on ensuring decent performance on lower-end hardware (including PC handhelds). With a 200-plus-gigabyte install size on consoles, I dread how big it’ll be on PC.

Ideally, the PC version will launch alongside an improved version of GTA Online (whether it’s free to play is anyone’s guess), and maybe with upgraded GTA roleplay tech to support it. I’m hopeful that the PC version of GTA VI will come in early 2027, but if the numerous delays of the console versions were any indication, the developer will take all the time it needs to get it right.

Upgrade, 9:55AM ET, November 19th: The SteamDB data cited now specifies that it’s concurrent users, not the number of users total.

Motorola has posted an updated list of devices getting its Android 17 revision, with a few updates already available and many more left to go.

With the update now rolling out to select devices, most recently the Razr Fold, Motorola is confirming an official list of devices getting Android 17.

The list was posted by Motorola Brazil, so this includes devices Motorola doesn’t sell in US markets, and also lists Razr devices without their year naming scheme, rather their international branding – i.e. “Razr (2026)” is “Razr 70.”.

In a recent development, as per usual, Motorola’s update rollouts may see timing vary by region. The Razr Fold update, for example, is currently rolling out in some international markets but has yet to land in the US.

Here’s the full list of Motorola devices officially confirmed to be getting Android 17:.

Motorola explains what’s newly introduced in Android 17 as follows:.

Among the upcoming features of Android 17 are improvements to the system interface, with more customization options, new icons, and changes to the layout of buttons and widgets. The Settings menu has been redesigned to make navigation more intuitive and facilitate access to the smartphone’s main functions.

Artificial intelligence in everyday life.

With the upgrade, Circle to Search now offers real-time translations, allowing you to understand content in other languages ​​more easily, without having to interrupt your current activity on your smartphone.

Simplified connectivity and sharing.

Android 17 enhances connectivity with Instant Hotspot , which simplifies sharing your internet connection between compatible devices. Quick Share has also received improvements to facilitate file transfer, including compatibility with iOS smartphones via QR Code.

Sources indicate that security remains a top priority for the system. The Authentication Failure Lock , a security feature in case of theft, locks the screen after unsuccessful authentication attempts. Meanwhile, Message-Based Fraud Detection enhances the identification of potential threats and fraud. Furthermore, access to emergency calls has become easier and faster.

More control over the visual experience.

The enhancement also improves HDR brightness control, which adjusts the screen intensity to highlight bright details in compatible photos and videos. Users can adjust this brightness for more comfortable viewing, or even disable the feature.

The Motorola Signature 27, the manufacturer’s new flagship, ships with Android 17 out of the box.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The console’s latest update finally activates its dormant Wi-Fi hardware, enabling a handful of upcoming features.

The console’s latest patch finally activates its dormant Wi-Fi hardware, enabling a handful of new features.

According to recent reports, analogue has long been good at expanding the features and functionality of its consoles through regular firmware updates, but installing those updates has always required moving files around with a memory card. That’s no longer the case with the Analogue 3D, the tech giant’s modernized version of the Nintendo 64. Although the console has had Wi-Fi hardware since day one, it’s only now been finally activated through the last update you’ll need to install with a memory card.

In a recent development, analogue on Wednesday released the version 1.6.0 firmware for the Analogue 3D, adding support for 2.4GHz, 5GHz, mixed, and hidden Wi-Fi networks. Once the update is installed, the Wi-Fi setup process will begin automatically when the console is booted, but there’s now an added Wi-Fi section in the Analogue 3D’s settings menu for updating passwords and other details later.

Sources indicate that the console’s new Wi-Fi capabilities add a couple of useful features at launch. In the future, the Analogue 3D will be able to download and install firmware updates so it automatically keeps itself up to date. The new wireless capabilities enable automatic date and time settings based on your time zone, too, and in the privacy section of the console’s settings menu, you’ll now find an option for sharing “anonymous usage and analytics data” with Analogue to help further improve its hardware.

Valve’s 512GB Steam Machine is available to buy now, but the 2TB model is out of stock.

In a recent development, if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Valve announced some updates about Steam Machine availability today, including good news if you want to buy one right now and potential bad news about future supply due to RAMaggedon.

The good news: You can now purchase a 512GB Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist. Initially, interested buyers had to get on Valve’s waitlist if they wanted to purchase one, but the console-like PC is now available in an “add-to-cart” status, according to the manufacturer. As I write this, the 512GB versions with and without a bundled controller are showing estimated delivery dates of three to five business days on Valve’s website. If Valve sells through its current inventory, the company states it will indicate that the product is out of stock instead of making another waitlist.

Recent findings suggest that the bad news: If you’re on the waitlist for a 2TB model, you might not get a chance to buy one at all, as Valve says there are more people on the waitlist than there are units available. The company is closing the waitlists for its 2TB models.

Valve says that while it’s still building more Steam machines, “memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels” and that it doesn’t know the number it can make or “at what price we’ll be able to offer them.” The 2TB Steam Machine is “especially constrained.” The company anticipates “having more information” to share about additional supply in January.

After delaying the Steam Machine’s expected early 2026 launch due to the memory and storage crisis, Valve launched the product in June with a price starting at $1,049 for the 512GB model without a bundled controller. A 2TB model without a controller costs $1,349.

I don't think much about the design of phones, they're essentially all the same, especially when considering you're looking at the front 90% of the time, but I've always found the Galaxy's vertical camera layout to be the least attractive of any of the major phones. I think this looks much better.

Xiaomi’s island is flat, following Google’s idea that a camera bar should protect the lenses and also keep the phone from wobbling or feeling off-balance.

Samsung has needed to change up the vertical camera bar for years, as it has regularly gotten in the way of Qi2 and MagSafe magnetic accessories. This newly introduced design might help that, but it seems fans wanted Samsung to return to the Galaxy S10 horizontal camera bar days, not this new iPhone-esque raised island.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, drones have become a major menace on modern battlefields, which is why Turkish defense firm Aselsan has developed a potent solution to counter them.
  • Recent findings suggest that while drones and uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) have been around for decades now, Russia’s 2022 escalation in Ukraine saw the first widespread use of small drones on the front line, some of which have been adapted from commercial models.
  • Many countries have started working on anti-drone defenses, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, drones have become a major menace on modern battlefields, which is why Turkish defense firm Aselsan has developed a potent solution to counter them. The company shared a YouTube video showing its Ejderha, which translates to “Dragon” in English Anti-Drone Countermeasure System taking down 51 drones simultaneously. The firm says that the device uses high-power electromagnetic (HPEM) waves and vacuum electronics to disable the electronic components on mini and micro drones.

Recent findings suggest that while drones and uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) have been around for decades now, Russia’s 2022 escalation in Ukraine saw the first widespread use of small drones on the front line, some of which have been adapted from commercial models. Because of this, we’ve seen various innovations in drone technologies, including the deployment of fiber optic drones to defeat radio jamming, the use of an onboard camera looking at a magnetic compass as a backup for GPS navigation, as well as the introduction of jam-resistant strike drones and “flying modems” that relay signals from one drone to another to extend their strike range.

Many countries have started working on anti-drone defenses, too. Ukraine has erected mobile barriers with rotating barbed wire designed to cut the fiber-optic lines that jam-proof Russian drones rely on, while various companies in the U.S.—from established players like Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman to startups like Mara—have been working on both airborne and ground-based solutions. China has also unveiled a man-portable design that neutralizes drones in under four seconds at up to 1,600 feet away using a 2-kilowatt laser.

Before the invention of the transistor in 1947, electronic devices relied on vacuum tubes, which were invented in 1904 by British engineer John Ambrose Fleming. Today, most devices rely on semiconductors for their power efficiency, reliability, and computing density. But if you need to produce a microwave signal strong enough to overwhelm the electronic components inside a drone, vacuum electronics is still one of the most effective solutions (although some companies are experimenting with solid-state semiconductors, too).

The U.S. and the UK are also working on their own HPEM systems, with the former testing the Leonidas Autonomous Ground Vehicle (AGV) and the latter trialing the Radio Frequency Directed Energy Weapon (RFDEW).

The game is finally here, and there’s plenty to discuss.

The game is finally here, and there’s plenty to discuss.

It’s hard to believe, but Grand Theft Auto VI is now a real thing that we all can play. Thirteen years after GTA V, and eight years since Red Dead Redemption 2, Rockstar is back with its latest sprawling, extravagant open world. There’s a lot to experience — and a lot to talk about.

Perhaps the most impressive thing about GTA VI is how flexible it is, letting you mold the experience to your own play style. You can still be a maniacal criminal, but you can also focus on the latest love story that includes an entire button dedicated to holding hands. Or you can spend the hours fishing or driving around listening to the radio. Maybe you just want to doomscroll through a fake version of Instagram. As GTA VI producer Rob Nelson told me just ahead of launch, “It’s a risk. It’s a real change for Grand Theft Auto. You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.”.

Now that the game is out and people are finding their own way through Leonida, it’s a great time to start talking about it. I’ve played through the entire main story — you can read my review right here — but I’m nowhere close to experiencing everything in the game. But I’m happy to answer any questions you have, though I’ll be careful around some of the significant story spoilers. I’ll also be joined by senior reporter Jay Peters, who is still early in the game and can offer a different perspective. There’s a good chance some other Verge staff will stop by as well, since we’re basically all playing it.

So drop all of your questions, theories, and stray thoughts about GTA VI here. I’ll be checking in throughout the day to join the conversation in the comments.

Picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

Shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that blueprint. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

Whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide indicates how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

Recent findings suggest that wooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

Recent findings suggest that bigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and plans auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the manufacturer notes you can export your data and self-host at any point.

It has been revealed that saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

Own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Knoxville Police Department has revealed its “Drone as First Responder” program, or DFR, with semi-autonomous drones set to be debuted from 12 docks located around the city.
  • According to recent reports, while the police department hasn't confirmed which drones will be used, we do know that they will be launched from Skydio docks located at city-owned facilities.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Knoxville Police Department has revealed its “Drone as First Responder” program, or DFR, with semi-autonomous drones set to be debuted from 12 docks located around the city. The docks will allow drones to be dispatched within seconds of a 911 call being received, and they will be able to reach nearly any area of the city within just 90 seconds, according to a page on the police department's website. It's hoped that the drones will be able to reduce the risk to the community as well as police officers, while providing real-time situational awareness during "rapidly evolving events.".

According to recent reports, while the police department hasn't confirmed which drones will be used, we do know that they will be launched from Skydio docks located at city-owned facilities. It's expected that the drones will, in some cases, reach the scene more quickly than the police officer they are supposed to accompany. This should give officers vital information related to the scene that they are about to attend.

It has been revealed that while drones won't be dispatched to all 911 calls, the department says that they will be sent in response to 911 calls in which aerial coverage may be of use to the overall response. That includes enhancing the safety of the officers attending as well as public safety.The upcoming drones will no doubt raise concerns about privacy. The department says that they will not be used for surveillance, pointing out that department policy and state law prohibit the drones from being used for random patrols or surveillance. They also don't possess any kind of facial recognition or license plate reader technologies. While the drones will, of course, capture video, the department's FAQ page notes that any recorded footage will be purged after 15 days. That is, unless it is retained as evidence for use in an ongoing criminal investigation or prosecution.

Sources indicate that knoxville isn't the first to turn to drones in this way. Several cities were reportedly experimenting with using Flock's own DFR system last month. Companies have also been advertising Starlink-connected first responder drones for some time.

  • Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app.
  • As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft announced this week that its To Do app is shutting down soon, taking the legacy of Wunderlist with it.

Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app. The tech giant explains:.

As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do. The To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027. Connections that other apps use to access To Do tasks will continue beyond that date, and we’ll provide separate notice before those connections are retired. We’re also updating existing task integrations across Microsoft 365 to connect with Planner, so you’ll be able to create or manage tasks in the Microsoft experiences you already use. Although To Do tasks are already visible in Planner, they will not be migrated to the upcoming private initiative. Customers using personal Microsoft accounts will need to choose another app. Our To Do transition guidance  will help you understand what’s changing and plan your next steps.

To Do was built on the foundation of Wunderlist, a wildly popular to do list app that Microsoft purchased in 2015. Wunderlist later shut down in 2020.

It has been revealed that microsoft’s shuffle, notably, leaves general consumers without a replacement app. To Do was available to anyone with a Microsoft account, where Planner is available only to enterprise/business people. So, for long-time Wunderlist users who followed Microsoft migration, this is the end of the road and it’s officially time to move to another app.

#69922. Gigabyte MO27Q2A 27-inch QHD 280 Hz QD-OLED gaming monitor review: Another price buster from Gigabyte

Gigabyte MO27Q2A 27-inch QHD 280 Hz QD-OLED gaming monitor review: Another price buster from Gigabyte

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Gigabyte MO27Q2A is a superlative value among 27-inch QHD OLEDs with high performance, accurate color and premium build quality.
  • Excellent build quality with mostly metal construction.
  • Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Gigabyte MO27Q2A is a superlative value among 27-inch QHD OLEDs with high performance, accurate color and premium build quality. It matches or exceeds many more expensive monitors.

Bright, sharp, and colorful picture.

Pro-level accuracy out of the box.

Useful Adobe RGB and sRGB color modes.

Tactical Switch for quick resolution changes.

Excellent build quality with mostly metal construction.

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

I have long stated that choices are important, and nowhere is that better illustrated than in the best OLED gaming monitor category. Once an exotic and expensive technology, it is now much more affordable, thanks to a plethora of upcoming models coming to market.

Gigabyte is certainly a leader in the price war with new models that deliver tremendous performance, image quality, and value. Its latest effort is a 27-inch QHD OLED model that refreshes at 280 Hz. It’s the MO27Q2A, and it leaves nothing out in its quest to be fast, beautiful, and packed with features. You get Adaptive-Sync with G-Sync and FreeSync certification, wide gamut color courtesy of Quantum Dot tech, HDR10, VESA DisplayHDR 400 True Black, USB ports with KVM, internal speakers and a better-than-average stand. Let’s take a look.

Quantum Dot Organic Light Emitting Diode (QD-OLED).

Max Resolution and Refresh Rate.

VESA DisplayHDR 400 True Black, HDR10.

If there’s one thing that the MO27Q2A leaves out, it's LED lighting. There’s no colorful show to dazzle your opponents with. But nothing else has been sacrificed. There are HDMI 2.1 ports, DisplayPort 1.4 with DSC (Display Stream Compression), USB-C that supports video and 18 watts of power, plus USB Type-A and Type-B ports with KVM control. A pair of five-watt internal speakers delivers good audio, or you can use the 3.5mm headphone jack.

The screen is super colorful with over 108% coverage of DCI-P3 thanks to a Quantum Dot layer. Color is very accurate, so much so that I found calibration completely unnecessary. You get sRGB and Adobe RGB options as well. Brightness is solid at 250 nits for a full field and over 1,000 nits for a 3% window pattern. You can use variable brightness for SDR and HDR content to pump up small highlights for even more dynamic range.

High-performance gaming is the primary goal here, and for that, the MO27Q2A comes with a reliable 280 Hz refresh rate, Adaptive-Sync with certifications from Nvidia and AMD, and a host of Game Assist features like aiming points, sniper modes, flash suppression, timers, and a frame counter. Like all OLEDs, it has lightning-fast reflexes with super smooth motion rendering.

Gigabyte pays plenty of attention to panel care with a host of options like pixel refresh and logo detection. There’s extensive passive cooling (no fans) and AI control that tracks usage at the pixel level to keep everything in balance. The end result is longevity and reliability, which is backed by a three-year factory warranty that includes burn-in.

According to recent reports, the MO27Q2A’s value is the most impressive part. At this writing, it sells for $399 online. It wasn’t long ago that you’d pay that for a 240 Hz QHD LCD. That category has dropped in cost as well, with some screens coming in around $200. But spending an extra $200 for an OLED seems like a no-brainer to me. Let’s see how the MO27Q2A fares in my tests.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Gigabyte offers a bit of fanfare on the MO27Q2A’s carton with colored graphics that set it apart from the plain brown wrappers more commonly seen at the major box store. A clamshell lid opens to reveal blocks of crumbly foam containing the panel, upright, and base, which assemble without tools. The power supply is internal, so you get a selection of IEC cords plus cables for HDMI, DisplayPort, and USB. A little clip goes on the stand to tidy up the wiring.

According to recent reports, the panel is minimalist from the front with a thin flush bezel and a metal backing that wraps around the edges. A narrow trim strip crosses the bottom with a tiny Gigabyte logo in its center. The controls are under the center point and consist of a backlit joystick and two keys. One is the Tactical Switch, and it changes resolutions on the fly. More about that below.

The stand is above average in quality with all-metal construction and smooth ergonomics. It includes 5.2 inches of height range plus 5/21 degrees tilt, 15 degrees swivel, and a 90-degree portrait mode. There is no hint of wobble or play. It is one of the better stands I’ve encountered, and I’ve encountered many.

From the side, you can see the panel-on-bulge design that is shared by many OLEDs. Not only does this look cool, but it actually is cool. The MO27Q2A’s panel is backed by metal, which acts as a heat sink. The bulge is also well ventilated, enough so that no fans are needed. A graphene layer behind the OLED contributes to cooling and hence, longevity.

Underneath is a well-appointed I/O panel with two HDMI 2.1s, a DisplayPort 1.4 with DSC, a USB-C that supports video and 18 watts of power, and USB 3.2, one upstream and two down. They can be bound to different video inputs using the KVM feature in the OSD. You also get a 3.5mm headphone jack and a pair of internal speakers with five watts of amplification.

The MO27Q2A’s OSD presents complete information with signal status at the top and current settings shown at the bottom.

Sources indicate that the Gaming menu includes a black frame insertion feature called Ultra Clear. It works at 280 or 120 Hz and is effective at removing motion blur. If you can run at 180fps or higher, you won’t need it. Other options include Black Equalizer, which increases shadow visibility, super resolution (edge enhancement, do not use), display mode for aspect ratio control, and a VRR toggle.

Recent findings suggest that the MO27Q2A includes 10 picture modes mainly aimed at different game types. It comes out of the box in Eco, which limits brightness. Choose Standard to unlock the maximum light output. Within this mode, you can adjust color temp and gamma and choose a color space. My sample was nearly perfect out of the box, so good, in fact, that I could not improve it with calibration. If you want sRGB or Adobe RGB color, those choices are in the Color Space submenu. For sRGB, there’s an sRGB picture mode. HDR signals get their own five modes. Peak 1000 is the brightest and best choice there.

In a recent development, you can use the KVM Wizard to bind USB ports and video inputs. That way, one keyboard, mouse, and monitor can service multiple sources like a PC and a gaming console, for instance. You can also view two sources at once using the PIP/PBP options.

Sources indicate that quick Switch lets the user program the functions of the joystick directionals. It provides quick access to commonly used functions like brightness or crosshairs.

A separate screen comes up for the MO27Q2A’s OLED care options. This is where you’ll find APL Stabilize, which has two levels of variable brightness or a constant setting. Its terminology is counterintuitive because Low means off, while Middle and High modulate light output more aggressively. High has the most dynamic range, with 1,000 peaks possible in HDR mode. If it were up to me, APL Stabilize would be in the Picture menu and be called Variable Brightness. Additional care options include pixel orbiting, panel refresh, and dimming for logos and corners. You turn any or all of these off if you wish.

It has been revealed that press the joystick and click right for the Game Assist menu and its plethora of play aids. You get four crosshairs, a timer, stopwatch, refresh rate indicator, and positioning of the information window. Also included are sniper mode and night vision. Flash Dimming suppresses your weapon’s muzzle flash if that becomes a distraction.

Gigabyte’s Tactical Switch is a unique feature that switches the MO27Q2A’s resolution on the fly. You can have FHD or HD in 16:9, 4:3, or 5:4 aspect ratios. The refresh rate remains at 280 Hz, but by shrinking the image, you get higher frame rates with no significant sharpness penalty.

Sources indicate that there isn’t much to the MO27Q2A’s calibration because it isn’t necessary. In fact, I could not improve my sample with calibration. It measures nearly perfect out of the box for D65, 2.2 gamma, and coverage of DCI-P3. The sRGB mode, which is also very accurate, is found in the picture mode list. For Adobe RGB, go to the Color Space sub-menu. For gaming and daily use, I settled on Standard mode, Native color space, and left everything else at default settings. My recommendations are below.

Sources indicate that for HDR signals, HDR is the default mode, but I found the same excellent accuracy and high brightness in the Peak 1000 mode. It delivers the promised 1,000 nits for a 3% window, which in my tests equated to 445 nits for a 25% window pattern. You get a number of sliders for brightness and contrast, but they are not needed unless you want a different look for HDR content.

A great way to evaluate a monitor’s HDR accuracy is by viewing static content that covers the full dynamic range of both color and neutral tones. Doom Eternal has such a screen in its HDR adjustment menu, and I use it for every review to verify detail rendering. The MO27Q2A showed every nuance in this torture test, which told me that it is very color accurate and tracks luminance correctly. In simple terms, you’ll see everything the game creators put in.

This gives gameplay a heightened sense of realism, especially in textures like stone, metal, and dirt. The MO27Q2A let me almost reach out and touch them. I had to remind myself that its resolution was QHD and Ultra HD because it rendered so finely. I also saw rich color that was perfectly balanced. You’ll see in the SDR and HDR tests that this is a seriously precise monitor.

Sources indicate that gameplay was up to the premium OLED standard with smooth motion that was completely free of blur. I had no trouble maintaining a constant 280fps. If you can’t hit that speed, Gigabyte includes Ultra Clear, which is a black frame insertion feature. It will remove motion blur at lower rates like 120 Hz. I noted that it was available at 280 Hz as well, which is unusual. It cuts brightness by around 40%, but you can partially compensate for that with the brightness slider. It operated artifact-free.

Another way to increase frame rates is with the Tactical Switch, which changes resolution and picture size on the fly. It doesn’t increase the refresh rate, but by shrinking the image, it maintains a favorable pixel map so that sharpness doesn’t take a huge hit.

According to recent reports, gameplay was addictive during my numerous frag fests. Input lag and response are super quick, which helped make my aim more precise. The MO27Q2A was so fast that it made me overconfident. I rushed into the melee rather than picking off enemies one by one. It was truly difficult to stop playing.

Sources indicate that the MO27Q2A excels as an everyday screen with 109ppi pixel density in its 27-inch form factor. It’s significantly less expensive than an Ultra HD monitor if you can accept a small reduction in clarity. And that resolution is a sweet spot for frame rates. You won’t need a giga-hauler video card to achieve its full potential.

Accurate color out of the box meant I could rely on the MO27Q2A as a reference for graphics and photos. I found excellent results in my initial tests, and I could not improve upon them with adjustments. This monitor is pro-level for sure.

Sources indicate that it’s impressive ergonomically too, with a solid all-metal stand and rugged panel construction. There are no missing features except for flashy LEDs. The internal speakers play loud and clear in the upper midrange, or you can plug in headphones. Users with a PC and console will appreciate the USB ports and KVM functions.

Takeaway: The MO27Q2A is a truly full-featured gaming monitor that can double as an everyday screen or a professional display. It games on par with the very best screens I’ve reviewed and delivers performance equal to more expensive OLEDs with higher refresh rates. It also matches those products in build quality with a solid stand and metal construction. For $399, you’ll be hard-pressed to find better.
