Recent findings suggest that good news first? Or bad news first?

According to recent reports, this is the final issue of What’s !notable on CSS-Tricks.com. The good news is that it’s coming back in an expanded form as the CSS-Tricks newsletter. I had ya there for a second, didn’t I? Sorry, I couldn’t decide whether to trick or treat, so I went for both. Happy Halloween!

Sources indicate that the newsletter officially kicks off on November 10th. That’s after a way-too-long four-year hiatus. What the heck, right? It’s not only high time for it to come back, but for you to get on the list. You’ll get hand-written and hand-curated news, links, and editorials that you can only find there. Join the party with me!

So, let’s go out with a big bang for our “final” issue. It’s packed with some stuff that I’ve been holding onto since before the site came back to life earlier this week, but also some new stuff, and I can’t wait to finally get it out to you.

Scooch over Apple, Rockstar has something they’d like to say about fancy scrolling effects (to be fair, they’ve had 13 years to create them). First, check out the GTA 6 website (which oddly doesn’t work in Firefox), then watch Kevin Powell’s GTA 6 scroll effects walkthrough, which is frankly the most fun that you can have while waiting (and waiting) for GTA 6.

Mojtaba Seyedi demonstrated how to build a scrollspy with modern CSS. What’s a scrollspy, you ask? Well, if you have a navigation that links to different sections of the page, a scrollspy highlights the section that you’re currently on in the navigation.

Brecht De Ruyte showcased and explained some absolutely stunning random() demos.

Okay, that was more than a few….

Recent findings suggest that lea Verou explained, in detail, the different ways of implementing icons on the web. Many exciting CSS features of the future are mentioned, including Linked Parameters, ident(), @mixin and @apply, the @property shorthand, and more, so it’s a really deep dive with a lot of intrigue.

According to recent reports, kilian Valkhof suggested a universal pseudo-selector. I mean, the universal selector (*) doesn’t select pseudo-elements, which is why almost every website uses the following CSS snippet, right?

But there are way more of them now (e.g., ::backdrop and ::details-content, to name just a couple of common ones in the context of box-sizing: border-box), so Kilian suggests ::*.

Industry observers note that declan Chidlow told us which new HTML and CSS features are useful for design systems. My favorites are text-box, sibling-index(), sibling-count(), @scope, and @custom-media, which are very handy even outside of design systems.

I am using the new if() syntax that allows me to define a condition within style(). If that condition is true, the background color is set to red. Otherwise, nothing happens.

The if() syntax is not that complex. In our case, we only have one condition, so you can see it as follows:.

Think for a moment about how to implement such a selector. It’s almost the same as the previous one.

If the index of the element is greater than or equal to the value of --B, the element is selected. As simple as that!

What about this one? Easy, right? We simply use <= instead of >=!

We can also easily implement a range selection, which is the combination of both selectors:.

According to recent reports, the code should be self-explanatory. It’s even more intuitive than the :nth-child() notation, which requires a few minutes of deciphering if you are not used to it.

It has been revealed that now let’s deal with the A argument. For example, the following selector:.

Recent findings suggest that …selects the 3rd, 6th, 9th, etc. elements. Seen differently, the index of the element needs to be a multiple of 3. To do such testing, we can use the mod() function. If mod(index, 3) returns 0, it means the remainder of the division of index by 3 is equal to 0, hence, it’s a multiple of 3.

It works! Another selector with a simple implementation.

We can identify two special cases. When --A is equal to 1, we have :nth-child(n), which selects all the elements and when it’s equal to 2, we have :nth-child(2n) which is also :nth-child(even).

While this works fine, there is a small gotcha. When A is a negative value, the selector should select nothing which is logical as all the indexes are positive, but if you try using negative values with my implementation, some elements still get selected which is wrong.

The mod() function works with negative numbers and can still return 0 in such cases, so to be more accurate, we should test the sign of A.

In a recent development, see that? I simply added another condition inside style() using the and keyword. The syntax of if() may sound confusing at first glance, but at the end it’s the same as any other language: a bunch of conditions defined inside style(). You can have as many as you want combined with and and or.

Now, our selection is more precise.

Recent findings suggest that now let’s combine all the tricks we learned so far to implement the generic form of :nth-child(). In this case, the index is equal to An + B, and we can express n like this:.

n should be a positive integer (zero included). For the positive part, we can use:.

For the integer part, we need to make sure index - B is a multiple of A, and for this, we use mod():.

We translate this into CSS to get the following:.

Recent findings suggest that we are almost good except for the case when --A is equal to 0. In that case, the selection is simply wrong. The mod() results in NaN since its second argument is equal to 0, and this will mess with the condition. Actually, that condition is not meant to work with --A equal to 0.

We either consider that this implementation is only valid for a value of --A different from 0 (which is probably what we want) or we try to find a solution to include that case.

Recent findings suggest that I hope you enjoyed this small exercise. It was a good opportunity to explore the new if() feature, and the :nth-child() selector was the perfect candidate for this. After all, selectors are nothing but a set of conditions to filter elements and select the needed ones.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I know there’s a lot of AI fatigue out there.
  • That’s why I’m stoked to check out Smashing’s AI conference on December 1.
  • And what makes those events the best is bringing in the best-of-the-best people to share what they’ve learned about it.

I know there’s a lot of AI fatigue out there. I feel it, too. Most of that though is more about the noise surrounding both sides of the hype spectrum. What’s covered way less is context for where it fits best in a development workflow and what sorts of practical uses it might have to benefit — not destroy — our work.

That’s why I’m stoked to check out Smashing’s AI conference on December 1. We all know Smashing. The good folks over there check the hype luggage at the door and give these sorts of landscape-changing things careful and thoughtful consideration. All their events, not to mention their articles, are that way and always have been. The best, really.

And what makes those events the best is bringing in the best-of-the-best people to share what they’ve learned about it. In this case we’re talking about a live online event specifically about AI in design systems from some of my personal favorite people, like Brad Frost, Christine Vallaure, Vitaly Friedman, and TJ Pitre. We’re talking about people who know their craft and the experience to show (not just tell) how it translates to what we do for work, whether you’re a designer, front-ender, or even a stakeholder in the design process.

In a recent development, so, please join me in checking it out. Cost is €50. They’re actually giving us here at CSS-Tricks a special discount using code AITRICKSCSS when you register for the event. Even better, they gave me two free tickets I’ll give to the first two commenters on this post. Just make sure you use your real email address when signing in to comment!
